raw.summary: Stack exhaustion in Decoder.Decode in encoding/gob
raw.details: Calling Decoder.Decode on a message which contains deeply nested structures can cause a panic due to stack exhaustion. This is a follow-up to CVE-2022-30635.

raw.summary: Timing sidechannel for P-256 on ppc64le in crypto/internal/nistec
raw.details: Due to the usage of a variable time instruction in the assembly implementation of an internal function, a small number of bits of secret scalars are leaked on the ppc64le architecture. Due to the way this function is used, we do not believe this leakage is enough to allow recovery of the private key when P-256 is used in any well known protocols.

raw.summary: Usage of ExtKeyUsageAny disables policy validation in crypto/x509
raw.details: Calling Verify with a VerifyOptions.KeyUsages that contains ExtKeyUsageAny unintentionally disabledpolicy validation. This only affected certificate chains which contain policy graphs, which are rather uncommon.

raw.summary: Sensitive headers not cleared on cross-origin redirect in net/http
raw.details: Proxy-Authorization and Proxy-Authenticate headers persisted on cross-origin redirects potentially leaking sensitive information.

credits.name: Takeshi Kaneko (GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae, Inc.)

raw.summary: Unexpected session resumption in crypto/tls
raw.details: During session resumption in crypto/tls, if the underlying Config has its ClientCAs or RootCAs fields mutated between the initial handshake and the resumed handshake, the resumed handshake may succeed when it should have failed. This may happen when a user calls Config.Clone and mutates the returned Config, or uses Config.GetConfigForClient. This can cause a client to resume a session with a server that it would not have resumed with during the initial handshake, or cause a server to resume a session with a client that it would not have resumed with during the initial handshake.

raw.summary: Memory exhaustion in query parameter parsing in net/url
raw.details:
The net/url package does not set a limit on the number of query parameters in a query.

While the maximum size of query parameters in URLs is generally limited by the maximum request header size, the net/http.Request.ParseForm method can parse large URL-encoded forms. Parsing a large form containing many unique query parameters can cause excessive memory consumption.

raw.summary: Incorrect enforcement of email constraints in crypto/x509
raw.details: When verifying a certificate chain which contains a certificate containing multiple email address constraints which share common local portions but different domain portions, these constraints will not be properly applied, and only the last constraint will be considered.

raw.summary: Incorrect parsing of IPv6 host literals in net/url
raw.details: url.Parse insufficiently validated the host/authority component and accepted some invalid URLs.

raw.summary: TOCTOU permits root escape on Linux via Root.Chmod in os in internal/syscall/unix
raw.details:
On Linux, if the target of Root.Chmod is replaced with a symlink while the chmod operation is in progress, Chmod can operate on the target of the symlink, even when the target lies outside the root.

The Linux fchmodat syscall silently ignores the AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW flag, which Root.Chmod uses to avoid symlink traversal. Root.Chmod checks its target before acting and returns an error if the target is a symlink lying outside the root, so the impact is limited to cases where the target is replaced with a symlink between the check and operation.

raw.summary: Case-sensitive excludedSubtrees name constraints cause Auth Bypass in crypto/x509
raw.details:
When verifying a certificate chain containing excluded DNS constraints, these constraints are not correctly applied to wildcard DNS SANs which use a different case than the constraint.

This only affects validation of otherwise trusted certificate chains, issued by a root CA in the VerifyOptions.Roots CertPool, or in the system certificate pool.

raw.summary: Miscompilation allows memory corruption via CONVNOP-wrapped array copy in cmd/compile
raw.details: The compiler is meant to unwrap pointers which are the operands of a memory move; a no-op interface conversion prevented the compiler from making the correct determination about non-overlapping moves, potentially leading to memory corruption at runtime.

raw.summary: Missing bound checks can lead to memory corruption in safe Go in cmd/compile
raw.details: Arithmetic over induction variables in loops were not correctly checked for underflow or overflow. As a result, the compiler would allow for invalid indexing to occur at runtime, potentially leading to memory corruption.

raw.summary: Unauthenticated TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate record can cause persistent connection retention and DoS in crypto/tls
raw.details:
If one side of the TLS connection sends multiple key update messages post-handshake in a single record, the connection can deadlock, causing uncontrolled consumption of resources. This can lead to a denial of service.

This only affects TLS 1.3.

raw.summary: Infinite loop in HTTP/2 transport when given bad SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE in net/http/internal/http2 in golang.org/x/net
raw.details: When processing HTTP/2 SETTINGS frames, transport will enter an infinite loop of writing CONTINUATION frames if it receives a SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE with a value of 0.

raw.summary: Inefficient policy validation in crypto/x509
raw.details:
Validating certificate chains which use policies is unexpectedly inefficient when certificates in the chain contain a very large number of policy mappings, possibly causing denial of service.

This only affects validation of otherwise trusted certificate chains, issued by a root CA in the VerifyOptions.Roots CertPool, or in the system certificate pool.

raw.summary: Unexpected work during chain building in crypto/x509
raw.details: During chain building, the amount of work that is done is not correctly limited when a large number of intermediate certificates are passed in VerifyOptions.Intermediates, which can lead to a denial of service. This affects both direct users of crypto/x509 and users of crypto/tls.

raw.summary: Quadratic string concatenation in consumePhrase in net/mail
raw.details: Pathological inputs could cause DoS through consumePhrase when parsing an email address according to RFC 5322.

raw.summary: Crash when handling long CNAME response in net
raw.details: When using LookupCNAME with the cgo DNS resolver, a very long CNAME response can trigger a double-free of C memory and a crash.

raw.summary: Quadratic string concatentation in consumeComment in net/mail
raw.details: Well-crafted inputs reaching ParseAddress, ParseAddressList, and ParseDate were able to trigger excessive CPU exhaustion and memory allocations.

raw.summary: Invoking failure to reject ASCII-only Punycode-encoded labels in golang.org/x/net/idna
raw.details:
The ToASCII and ToUnicode functions incorrectly accept Punycode-encoded labels that decode to an ASCII-only label. For example, ToUnicode("xn--example-.com") incorrectly returns the name "example.com" rather than an error.

This behavior can lead to privilege escalation in programs using the idna package. For example, a program which performs privilege checks on the ASCII hostname may reject "example.com" but permit "xn--example-.com". If that program subsequently converts the ASCII hostname to Unicode, it will inadvertently permits access to the Unicode name "example.com".

raw.summary: Invoking incorrect handling of HTML elements in foreign content in golang.org/x/net/html
raw.details: Parsing arbitrary HTML which is then rendered using Render can result in an unexpected HTML tree. This can be leveraged to execute XSS attacks in applications that attempt to sanitize input HTML before rendering.

raw.summary: Invoking incorrect handling of character references in DOCTYPE nodes in golang.org/x/net/html
raw.details: Parsing arbitrary HTML which is then rendered using Render can result in an unexpected HTML tree. This can be leveraged to execute XSS attacks in applications that attempt to sanitize input HTML before rendering.

raw.summary: Invoking duplicate attributes can cause XSS in golang.org/x/net/html
raw.details: Parsing arbitrary HTML which is then rendered using Render can result in an unexpected HTML tree. This can be leveraged to execute XSS attacks in applications that attempt to sanitize input HTML before rendering.

raw.summary: Inefficient candidate hostname parsing in crypto/x509
raw.details:
(*x509.Certificate).VerifyHostname previously called matchHostnames in a loop over all DNS Subject Alternative Name (SAN) entries. This caused strings.Split(host, ".") to execute repeatedly on the same input hostname.

With a large DNS SAN list, verification costs scaled quadratically based on the number of SAN entries multiplied by the hostname's label count. Because x509.Verify validates hostnames before building the certificate chain, this overhead occurred even for untrusted certificates.

raw.summary: Quadratic complexity in WordDecoder.DecodeHeader in mime
raw.details: Decoding a maliciously-crafted MIME header containing many invalid encoded-words can consume excessive CPU.

raw.summary: Infinite loop on invalid input in golang.org/x/text
raw.details: A norm.Iter can enter an infinite loop when handling input containing invalid UTF-8 bytes.

raw.summary: Enforce maximum recursion depth in encoding/asn1
raw.details: Enforce a recursion limit in Unmarshal to prevent stack exhaustion when parsing deeply-nested, recursive structures.

raw.summary: Add recursion depth guard during decode in encoding/xml
raw.details: Previously, DecodeElement would reset the depth counter causing it to never fire; this could lead to stack exhaustion.

raw.summary: Apply ReadHeaderTimeout when doing unencrypted HTTP/2 check in net/http
raw.details: When a server is configured to support unencrypted HTTP/2, it reads a few bytes from each new connection to see if they contain the HTTP/2 client preface. ReadHeaderTimeout is unexpectedly not being applied when doing this.

raw.summary: Limit handshake messages we are willing to accept post-handshake in crypto/tls
raw.details: Handshake messages, such as KeyUpdate, are always considered as state-advancing, regardless of whether a handshake has been completed or not. As a result, a malicious client can keep sending KeyUpdate messages to force the server to keep performing key derivation operations indefinitely.

raw.summary: Fix Javascript regexp context tracking in html/template
raw.details: Previously, pathological inputs could close an unescaped '/' early, allowing for attack-controlled data to inject arbitrary content, potentially leading to XSS.

raw.summary: Avoid quadratic complexity in resolvePath in net/url
raw.details:
Previously, resolving relative paths containing parent directory ('..') segments performed string conversions and buffer rewrites on each step, resulting in quadratic time complexity and high memory allocation overhead.

Now, path resolution operates on a byte buffer using index-based backtracking for '..' segments, eliminating the quadratic time complexity and significantly reducing memory allocations.

raw.summary: Prevent DoS on deadlocked established channel in golang.org/x/crypto/ssh
raw.details:
Previously, after a channel has been established, a malicious peer could send crafted messages that would deadlock the entire connection.

Now, we handle all RFC 4254 channel messages; global requests are handled explicitly. Then, treat all other messages as a protocol error and tear the connection down instead of buffering and blocking.

raw.summary: Unexpected code execution via escaped quotes in //go:cgo_ldflag in cmd/go and cmd/compile
raw.details:
Building a malicious package that uses cgo could bypass "#cgo LDFLAGS" validation and cause unexpected code execution at build time, or cause the go command to panic, via crafted quoting in "//go:cgo_ldflag" directives.

When "cmd/cgo" generates "_cgo_gotypes.go", it quotes each "#cgo LDFLAGS" argument with strconv.Quote in a "//go:cgo_ldflag" directive, but "cmd/compile" and "cmd/go" parsed those directives by splitting on raw quote characters without handling backslash escapes or unquoting the string. This mismatch allowed disallowed linker flags or unvalidated linker search paths to be smuggled past the go command's flag checks and passed to the external linker. In addition, deduplicating LDFLAGS in the go command could panic with an out-of-bounds slice index when a prefix of the flag list matched near the end of the slice.

"cmd/compile" and "cmd/go" now properly handle backslash-escaped quotes and unquote "//go:cgo_*" pragma strings with strconv.Unquote, and the slice bounds check in processCgoOutputs has been fixed.

raw.summary: Linker flag injection via cgo_import_dynamic and PE DLL names in cmd/cgo, cmd/compile, and cmd/link
raw.details:
Building a malicious package that uses "//go:cgo_import_dynamic" or links against a crafted PE object on Windows could pass unsafe library arguments to the external linker.

The compiler only checked the first character of the library name in "//go:cgo_import_dynamic" directives and skipped validation in cgo-generated files. In addition, on Windows, "cmd/cgo" and "cmd/link" did not validate imported DLL names extracted from PE object files before emitting "-l<name>" flags for the external linker, allowing a crafted DLL name containing ".." path traversal or special characters to reference arbitrary files on disk.

The compiler now validates every character of the library name in "//go:cgo_import_dynamic" directives (including in cgo-generated files on Windows) and rejects ".." path traversal, and "cmd/cgo" and "cmd/link" reject PE imported DLL names containing path separators, "..", ":", or leading "-" or "@".

raw.summary: Host linker flag injection via //go:cgo_* directives in cmd/compile and cmd/link
raw.details:
Building a malicious package containing "//go:cgo_*" compiler directives could inject arbitrary flags into the external linker invocation on ELF platforms.

The compiler and linker did not reject commas in "//go:cgo_import_dynamic", "//go:cgo_export_dynamic", "//go:cgo_export_static", "//go:cgo_import_static", and "//go:cgo_dynamic_linker" directives, and the linker passed the dynamic linker path using "-Wl,--dynamic-linker,<path>". Furthermore, the two-argument form of "//go:cgo_import_dynamic" (which is permitted in non-cgo Go source files) could overwrite the external symbol name of a symbol already marked for cgo export. A symbol name or dynamic linker path containing a comma or leading "@" could split "-Wl,--export-dynamic-symbol=" or "-Wl,--dynamic-linker," into arbitrary host linker flags or response file arguments.

The compiler and linker now reject commas in "//go:cgo_*" symbol and dynamic linker directives, the linker passes "-Wl,--dynamic-linker=<path>", and "cgo_import_dynamic" no longer overwrites symbols exported via "cgo_export_dynamic" or "cgo_export_static".

credits.name: RyotaK (https://ryotak.net) of GMO Flatt Security Inc.

raw.summary: Cgo directive injection via .syso files disguised as Go object files in cmd/go and cmd/link
raw.details:
Building a package containing a crafted ".syso" file could bypass cgo flag validation and inject arbitrary linker flags when linking.

When loading ".syso" entries from a package archive, the linker only checked for recognized host object headers (ELF, Mach-O, PE, and XCOFF) before falling through to Go object parsing. A ".syso" file beginning with a "go object" header was parsed as a Go compiler object, allowing untrusted cgo metadata directives (such as "cgo_ldflag" or "cgo_dynamic_linker") embedded in the ".syso" file to be passed to the external linker without validation. Additionally, ".syso" filenames longer than 16 bytes lost their ".syso" extension when truncated in archive headers, and unrecognized ".syso" formats forced external linking in pure-Go builds.

The linker now rejects ".syso" files that are not recognized host object formats, and "cmd/go" and "cmd/pack" preserve the ".syso" suffix when truncating long archive member names.

credits.name: RyotaK (https://ryotak.net) of GMO Flatt Security Inc.

raw.summary: Flag sanitization bypass via "#cgo pkg-config:" directives in cmd/go
raw.details:
Building a malicious package that uses "#cgo pkg-config:" directives could load untrusted pkg-config ".pc" files or inject unvalidated compiler and linker flags.

The pkg-config flag allowlist previously permitted "--with-path=" and "--personality=", allowed "--define-variable=" values beginning with "=" or "$" (which can rewrite paths in system ".pc" files into sysroot-prefixed "-L=" or "-L$SYSROOT" linker search paths), and allowed package arguments ending in ".pc" or containing path separators or "..", which caused pkg-config to load local ".pc" files directly from the package directory. In addition, flags returned by "pkg-config --cflags" in cgoCPPFLAGS were not checked when determining whether internal linking is safe.

The go command now disallows "--with-path=", "--personality=", leading "=" or "$" characters in "--define-variable=" values, and local ".pc" paths in "#cgo pkg-config:" directives, and inspects cgoCPPFLAGS when checking internal linking compatibility.

raw.summary: Arbitrary code execution via crafted .syso files and cgo linker input files in cmd/go
raw.details:
Building a malicious package containing ".syso" files or cgo linker inputs could inject arbitrary linker flags or execute arbitrary code at link time.

Linker input files—including ".syso" files, direct object or library inputs in "#cgo LDFLAGS", and libraries in "-L" directories—were passed to the external linker without validating their format or checking for embedded linker options. Across platforms, this allowed executing GNU ld implicit linker scripts disguised as libraries or ".syso" files (or loaded via "-l:<filename>" or "-l" containing path separators), injecting unallowlisted linker flags via PE/COFF ".drectve" sections on Windows or Mach-O "LC_LINKER_OPTION" load commands on Darwin, or invoking LTO plugins via GCC or LLVM LTO intermediate representation sections in ELF, PE/COFF, or Mach-O objects.

The go command now verifies that ".syso" files, direct linker inputs, and libraries in "-L" directories are valid binary objects or archives that do not contain unallowlisted ".drectve" directives, "LC_LINKER_OPTION" load commands, or LTO IR sections, and disallows "-l:<filename>" and ":", "=", or path separators in "-l" flags.

raw.summary: Linker script injection via split -Wl, flags and Darwin or symbol linker flags in cgo in cmd/go
raw.details:
Building a malicious package that uses cgo could cause arbitrary code execution at link time by passing linker script files to the host linker via "#cgo LDFLAGS".

Split "-Wl," flags that consume a following argument (such as "-Wl,-rpath", "-Wl,--just-symbols", and "-Wl,-undefined") previously accepted a bare second argument without a "-Wl," prefix, which the compiler driver passes directly to the linker as a positional input file. Additionally, when using GNU ld.bfd, flags such as "-framework", "-Wl,-framework", "-Wl,-undefined", "-Wl,--just-symbols", "-Wl,-R", "-Wl,-subsystem", and (on non-Darwin platforms) "-Wl,-sectcreate" could cause ld.bfd to interpret their arguments as linker scripts if they named a regular file on disk.

The go command now requires a "-Wl," prefix on the second token of split "-Wl," flags (except "-Wl,-R"), verifies that these flags do not reference linker script files, and disallows bare "-Wl,--warn-backrefs-exclude".

raw.summary: Arbitrary code execution during build on darwin via "-l to_library" in cgo in cmd/go
raw.details:
On Darwin, building a malicious package that uses cgo could cause arbitrary code execution when using the Apple linker due to passing "-l to_library <path>" in a "#cgo LDFLAGS" directive.

The Apple linker recombines the separated arguments "-l" and "to_library" into "-lto_library", which loads an arbitrary LTO plugin dynamic library at link time.

The go command now disallows "-l" followed by "to_library" in "#cgo LDFLAGS", rejects "-lazy_library", "-lazy_framework", "-load_hidden", "-library", and "-library-path", and checks recombined "-l" arguments against disallowed linker flags and patterns.

raw.summary: Unexpected code execution and arbitrary file write via Clang -gen-* and GCC -gnat* flags in cgo in cmd/go
raw.details:
When using Clang or GCC, building a malicious package that uses cgo could cause unexpected code execution at build time or write files to arbitrary directories via "-gen-*" or "-gnat*" flags in "#cgo" directives.

The "-g*" wildcard in the compiler and linker flag allowlists previously matched Clang's two-argument "-gen-cdb-fragment-path <dir>" flag and GCC's two-argument "-gnatO <file>" flag, permitting compilation database fragments and sidecar output files to be written to arbitrary directories and desynchronizing flag argument parsing between the go command and the compiler driver so that subsequent arguments could be passed as unvalidated positional inputs to the linker.

"-gen-*" and "-gnat*" flags are now disallowed in "#cgo" compiler and linker flags.

raw.summary: Arbitrary command execution via GCC spec files in cgo linker search directories in cmd/go
raw.details:
When using GCC, building a malicious package that uses cgo could cause arbitrary command execution at link time via untrusted GCC spec files ("specs" or "*.spec").

When linking with "-fopenmp", "-fopenacc", or "-fsanitize=" in "#cgo LDFLAGS", GCC's built-in link spec evaluates "%:include(libgomp.spec)" or "%:include(libsanitizer.spec)" and searches for spec files in "-L" and sysroot directories (including subdirectories and multilib sibling directories such as "../lib64"), as well as the working directory when "-fopenmp" or "-fopenacc" is used or when "-fsanitize=" is combined with "-static" or "-static-lib*".

The go command now rejects "-L", "-isysroot", and "-Wl,-syslibroot" directories (and the working and package directories when applicable) that contain GCC spec files, and disallows "@" and "-" prefixes in "-fsanitize=" compiler flag values.

raw.summary: Unexpected code execution via --sysroot, -target, -isysroot, -Wl,-syslibroot, and -x cgo flags in cmd/go
raw.details:
Building a malicious package that uses cgo could cause arbitrary code execution at build time through several compiler and linker flags permitted in "#cgo" directives.

Specifically, "--sysroot" in GCC and Clang relocates compiler subprograms, spec files, and CRT startup objects to an attacker-controlled directory; "-target" in Clang falls back to executing target helper tools from the current working directory when not found in PATH; "-isysroot" and "-Wl,-syslibroot" can pass a regular file on disk to GNU ld.bfd, which interprets it as a positional linker script; and "-x" permitted specifying arbitrary compiler input languages beyond those supported by cgo.

"--sysroot" and "-target" are now disallowed in "#cgo" flags, "-isysroot" and "-Wl,-syslibroot" are verified not to point to regular files, and "-x" is restricted to the C, C++, Objective-C, and assembler languages supported by cgo.

raw.summary: HTTP/1 server crash due to MaxBytesReader header race in net/http
raw.details: For HTTP/1 servers, when MaxBytesReader's limit is exceeded, "Connection: close" header is automatically set without synchronization, which might race with another header being set explicitly in the server handler. As a result, an HTTP/1 server that utilizes MaxBytesReader or MaxBytesHandler can crash due to runtime panic if its handler reads the request body concurrently with writing the response header.

raw.summary: Unsoundness in UTF-8 'String' trait
raw.details:
The String API in iceoryx2-bb-container exposes its contents as mutable bytes through safe APIs, while String::as_str() converts those bytes into a Rust string slice without validating UTF-8. 
An application can therefore create an invalid &str and trigger undefined behavior using entirely safe Rust.

The API methods `as_mut_bytes` and `deref_mut` where removed from the String API and their implementations (PolymorphicString, RelocatableString, and StaticString ) without replacement.
Link to Pull-Request: https://github.com/eclipse-iceoryx/iceoryx2/pull/1956

raw.summary: Panic on a GCP launch endorsement without TDX measurements
raw.details:
`GcpTdxHost::verify_launch_endorsement()`, available with the `host-gcp-tdx`
feature, read `uefi_golden.tdx.measurements[0]` without checking that the
golden measurement contains a TDX measurement. If a launch endorsement's
golden measurement had no TDX measurements, the call panicked with an index
out of bounds instead of returning an error.

The panic is reached only after the endorsement's signing certificate and
signature have been verified. Triggering it therefore requires a correctly
signed endorsement that lacks TDX measurements.

Intel describes the issue as improper input validation and classifies it as
denial of service, with a CVSS 4.0 base score of 5.7, in INTEL-SA-01520.

The flaw was corrected in
[#87](https://github.com/IntelLabs/tdx-workload-attestation/pull/87), released
in 0.2.0. The function now returns `Error::ParseError` when the TDX
measurement structure is missing or empty.

Reported by [Borys Tsyrulnikov](https://borystsyrulnikov.dev).

raw.summary: `verify_x509_cert` does not check the certificate validity period
raw.details:
`tdx_workload_attestation::verification::x509::verify_x509_cert()`, available
with the `host-verification` feature, checked that `issuer_cert` issued `cert`
and verified the certificate signature. It did not check the certificate's
validity period, so it accepted expired and not-yet-valid certificates.

With the `host-gcp-tdx` feature, this function validates the GCP launch
endorsement signing certificate against the GCE confidential-computing TCB
root certificate. A signing certificate outside its validity period was
therefore still accepted during launch endorsement verification.

Intel describes the issue as improper certificate validation and classifies
it as escalation of privilege, with a CVSS 4.0 base score of 5.9, in
INTEL-SA-01520.

The flaw was corrected in
[#86](https://github.com/IntelLabs/tdx-workload-attestation/pull/86), released
in 0.2.0. The function now returns `Ok(false)` when the current time is
outside the certificate's `notBefore`/`notAfter` range.

Reported by [Borys Tsyrulnikov](https://borystsyrulnikov.dev).

raw.summary: Paths or symlinks ending in a slash escape the sandbox
raw.details:
cap-primitives resolves a path inside a sandboxed directory one component at a time and opens the last component with `O_NOFOLLOW`, so that a symlink there cannot lead out of the directory. When the path ended in `/`, the resolver added the slash back to the last component before opening it. With a trailing slash the operating system no longer treats that component as the last one, so `O_NOFOLLOW` does not apply, the symlink is followed, and the resulting file descriptor was returned without further checks.

A symlink inside the sandbox that points outside it, such as `escape -> ../outside` or a link to `/`, can therefore be opened as `escape/`. If the symlink's own target ends in `/`, the caller's path does not need a trailing slash at all, so removing trailing slashes from untrusted input is not a workaround. The maintainers' advisory reports reads and writes outside the sandbox through `open`, `open_dir`, `read_dir` and `canonicalize`, and directory creation, removal and renames outside it through `create_dir`, `remove_dir` and `rename`.

This resolver is used on Windows and macOS, on FreeBSD when `O_RESOLVE_BENEATH` is not available, and on Linux when `openat2` is not available (kernels before 5.6, or a seccomp policy that rejects it). cap-std and other crates built on cap-primitives are affected through it. Wasmtime's WASI filesystem support was affected as well; that is covered by RUSTSEC-2026-0269.

The fix stops re-adding the trailing slash and is in 3.4.6 and 4.0.3.

raw.summary: `lwd-uri-util` was removed from crates.io for malicious code
raw.details:
The `lwd-uri-util` crate exfiltrated SSH keys, AWS credentials, and other
environmental metadata and secrets when any crate using it was built.

The malicious crate had 8 versions published on 2026-11-09 approximately 12
hours before removal and had no evidence of actual usage. This crate had no
dependencies on crates.io.

Thanks to [Bitbison](https://bitbison.io/) for the report.

raw.summary: Inverted bitmap validation in `invalidate_l2_cached_ept`
raw.details:
`tdx_guest::tdcall::invalidate_l2_cached_ept()` takes a bitmap that selects the
L2 VMs whose cached EPT translations should be invalidated. Bits 1 through 3
select L2 VMs 1 through 3, and all other bits are reserved. The input check
was inverted:

    if l2_vm_idx_bitmap & !0b1110 == 0 {
        return Err(TdCallError::TdxOperandInvalid);
    }

`l2_vm_idx_bitmap & !0b1110` isolates the bits that are not allowed. A result
of zero means the bitmap is valid, and the function returned an error in that
case. Every valid bitmap, such as `0b0010` or `0b1110`, was therefore rejected
with `TdxOperandInvalid`. Bitmaps with reserved bits set, such as `0b0001` or
`0b1_0000`, were forwarded to the TDX module.

Intel describes the issue as an incorrect comparison and classifies it as
escalation of privilege, with a CVSS 4.0 base score of 4.6, in
INTEL-SA-01462.

The flaw was corrected in commit
[`311d33b`](https://github.com/intel/confidential-computing.tdx.tdx-guest/commit/311d33b18a5bef5dc67c9b0c86587dd00c77027e),
released in 0.3.1. The function now rejects an empty bitmap and any bit
outside `0b1110`.

Reported by [Borys Tsyrulnikov](https://borystsyrulnikov.dev).

raw.summary: `enter_l2_vcpu` passes the wrong RCX operand to `TDG.VP.ENTER`
raw.details:
`tdx_guest::tdcall::enter_l2_vcpu()` invokes the `TDG.VP.ENTER` TDCALL. RCX
must carry the L2 VM index in bits 53:52 and the invalidation control value
(`InvdTranslations`, 0 to 3) in bits 1:0. The function computed that value as
`(l2_vm_idx << 52) | (invd_translations as u64)`, but then passed the raw
`l2_vm_idx` in RCX instead.

As a result, the TDX module received an operand that differs from the
caller's request. The VM index field was 0, and the low bits of the index
were interpreted as the invalidation control value. For example, VM 1 with
`InvdTlb` (2) should produce `0x0010_0000_0000_0002`, but produced `0x1`.

Intel describes the issue as an incorrect calculation and classifies it as
escalation of privilege, with a CVSS 4.0 base score of 4.6, in
INTEL-SA-01462.

The flaw was corrected in commit
[`311d33b`](https://github.com/intel/confidential-computing.tdx.tdx-guest/commit/311d33b18a5bef5dc67c9b0c86587dd00c77027e),
released in 0.3.1, which passes the computed RCX value.

Reported by [Borys Tsyrulnikov](https://borystsyrulnikov.dev).

raw.summary: xattr functions mark unwritten bytes as initialized when given a zero-length buffer
raw.details:
The extended-attribute functions in `rustix::fs` (`getxattr`, `lgetxattr`, `fgetxattr`, `listxattr`, `llistxattr` and `flistxattr`) write into a `Buffer` and then mark as many bytes initialized as the system call reported. When the buffer has zero length, the operating system treats the call as a size query: it writes nothing and returns the size of the attribute value or of the name list. rustix still marked that many bytes as initialized.

Passing a `Vec` whose length equals its capacity through `spare_capacity` gives such a zero-length buffer, and rustix then set the vector's length past its capacity over memory that was never written. This is undefined behavior reachable from safe code. With an empty `&mut [MaybeUninit<u8>]` the call panics instead.

From 1.1.6 these functions return an empty result for a zero-length buffer, and new `getxattr_query`, `lgetxattr_query`, `fgetxattr_query`, `listxattr_query`, `llistxattr_query` and `flistxattr_query` functions return the size. The 0.38 series did not have the `Buffer` API and is not affected.

raw.summary: Panic on a malformed `alpn` value when parsing SVCB or HTTPS records from text
raw.details:
When an SVCB or HTTPS record is parsed from its text (zone file) form, the `alpn` service parameter value is split into a list of protocol names. That step called `expect` on the result, on the assumption that it could not fail. A malformed value, such as one with an unbalanced quote (`alpn="h`), two commas in a row or an invalid escape, makes it fail, so the parser panicked instead of returning an error.

Code that parses zone files or record text from an untrusted source can be made to panic, which is a denial of service. Records decoded from the DNS wire format are not parsed this way.

The fix returns a parse error instead. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Integer underflow when reporting a malformed TSIG record
raw.details:
When a TSIG record is decoded from the DNS wire format, its MAC length and "other data" length are checked against the end of the record data. If a check failed, the error value was built from `end_idx - decoder.index()`. For a malformed record the decoder can already be past `end_idx`, so this unsigned subtraction underflows.

In builds with overflow checks enabled (the `dev` profile by default) the underflow panics, so a peer that sends a crafted TSIG record can crash the process. In builds without overflow checks the result wraps and is only used in the returned error.

The fix returns a plain "insufficient bytes" error without the subtraction. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Panic when an SVCB or HTTPS parameter value is a single quote character
raw.details:
When an SVCB or HTTPS record is parsed from its text (zone file) form, surrounding double quotes are removed from each service parameter value by checking that the value starts and ends with `"` and slicing off the first and last character. A value that is a single `"` (for example `alpn="`) passes that check, and the slice `[1..0]` panics.

Code that parses zone files or record text from an untrusted source can be made to panic, which is a denial of service. Records decoded from the DNS wire format are not parsed this way.

The fix rejects a lone quote character with a parse error before the slice. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Zone file lexer panics on a token of 4096 or more characters
raw.details:
The zone file lexer read each token in a loop capped at 4,096 iterations, with an `assert!` on the loop counter as a safety bound. A single token long enough to reach that bound, for example a very long name or character string in a zone file, triggered the assertion and the parser panicked instead of returning the token or an error.

Code that parses zone files from an untrusted source can be made to panic, which is a denial of service.

The fix removes the iteration bound, so the lexer ends only when it reaches the end of a token or an error. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Memory amplification from record counts in the DNS message header
raw.details:
When a DNS message is decoded, the vectors for the question, answer, authority and additional sections were created with `Vec::with_capacity` set to the counts in the message header. Those counts come from the sender and are not checked against the size of the message, so a single small packet that claims 65,535 records makes the decoder reserve memory for that many records (about 18 MB, according to the upstream advisory) before it reads any record and fails.

Any code that decodes untrusted DNS messages is exposed. That includes servers, and clients and resolvers that receive spoofed responses. Repeated packets can drive memory use up and cause a denial of service.

The fix caps the initial capacity at 8 entries and lets the vectors grow as records are actually decoded. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Transaction::from_json holds an input txid that is not 64 hex digits and writes the input as spending the zero txid
raw.details:
`Transaction::from_json`, for a document with no `hex` member, held each
input's `txid` member as given. An input `txid` that is not 64 hex digits
(`"zz"`, `""`, 63 or 65 digits, characters that are not hex digits) answered
`Ok`: `source_txid` and `to_json` gave the text back, while `to_binary` wrote
the input as spending the txid of 32 zero bytes and `id()` hashed those bytes.
Documents naming different texts were one transaction, spending an outpoint
none of them named.

An application that reads a peer's transaction document with `from_json` and
relies both on the text of its inputs and on its bytes or `id()` is affected;
one that reads only documents it produced is not.

0.8.6 refuses such a txid (`Invalid txid of input N: expected 64 hex digits`).
Where upgrading is not possible, require each input's `txid` to be 64 ASCII hex
digits before calling `from_json`.

raw.summary: Transaction readers accept trailing bytes, so a parsed transaction can carry another transaction id
raw.details:
`Transaction::from_binary` and `Transaction::from_hex` read one transaction
from the front of their input, did not check that the input ended there, and
kept the whole input as the transaction's cached serialization: `to_binary`,
`to_hex` and `id()` then answered for bytes that are not the transaction's.
`Transaction::from_json`, given a `hex` field, reads it through `from_hex` and
answers the same. `from_ef`, `from_hex_ef` and `parse_script_offsets` also
read a prefix.

An application that takes bytes or hex from outside, parses them with these
readers and then uses `id()` or the serialization could be given one
transaction under another identity: the same parsed fields, a different id.
An application that passes them only bytes it produced or has already checked
is not affected.

0.8.5 refuses a byte after the transaction; `Transaction::from_reader` reads
from the front of a longer buffer. Where upgrading is not possible, parse with
`Transaction::from_binary`, call `tx.invalidate_caches()` (public from 0.3.16)
and require `tx.to_binary() == bytes`.

raw.summary: Signature::from_der reads a signature with bytes after it, a wrong sequence length or an unneeded zero as the signature
raw.details:
`Signature::from_der` read a DER-encoded ECDSA signature leniently. It read as
the signature: the signature followed by other bytes; a sequence length
shorter than its contents, or longer with bytes after them (a length byte with
its high bit set among them); and an R or S preceded by a zero byte it did not
need. It read a lone-zero R or S as zero.

`messages::verify`, `compat::bsm::verify_message_der`,
`auth::Certificate::verify`, `auth::VerifiableCertificate::verify`,
`wallet::ProtoWallet::verify_signature` and
`kvstore::KVStoreInterpreter::verify_signature` read through it, and each
verified such a form of a valid signature. Given one signature a key holder
made, anyone could produce other byte strings that verify as that signature
over the same data. No form verifies over other data: an application that acts
on the verdict alone is not affected; one that compares, hashes or stores a
signature's bytes is.

0.8.6 refuses each form as `Error::InvalidSignature`. A signature's bytes are
still not unique after the patch: the same signature with S replaced by n - S
verifies, so an application that keys on the bytes also requires
`Signature::is_low_s()`.

raw.summary: BEEF validation answers valid for a raw entry that is not a transaction
raw.details:
`Beef::merge_raw_tx` and `BeefTx::from_raw_tx` accept raw bytes without a
`Result`. For bytes that are not exactly one transaction (a transaction
followed by bytes, a cut transaction, bytes that are no transaction at all),
`Beef::sort_txs`, `verify_structure`, `verify_valid` and `is_valid` could
answer valid, even with no BUMP and no parent in the BEEF, and, where the entry
carried a BUMP index, treat the hash of those bytes as a proven transaction id;
an entry that names it as a parent was answered valid too.

The wire readers (`Beef::from_binary`, `verify_stream`,
`Transaction::from_beef`, `from_atomic_beef`) parse every entry and are not
affected. Reaching this needs an application that passes bytes it did not
parse to `merge_raw_tx` or `BeefTx::from_raw_tx` and then relies on the verdict
or on the transaction the BEEF hands back.

0.8.5 refuses such an entry at all four verdict doors, with or without a BUMP
index, and every entry that names it as a parent. Where upgrading is not
possible, do not rely on `is_valid` or `verify_valid` alone for such an entry:
check that the bytes are exactly one transaction before merging them.

raw.summary: Shamir backup recovery accepts a share at x = 0, so a supplied share can substitute the recovered private key
raw.details:
`KeyShares::from_backup_format` (the Shamir backup share reader, public since
0.2.0, the crate's first release) accepted a share whose x coordinate is 0,
and `KeyShares::recover_private_key` interpolates the shares at x = 0 to
recover the key. At an x of 0 the interpolation answers that share's y value
alone, so an attacker who supplies one share in that form — with the share's
integrity tag ground to match the honest set's — chooses the recovered key
outright. The non-canonical zero x = p works the same way, and a repeated x
past the threshold window also passed.

An application that recovers a Shamir backup from shares it did not produce —
a custodian's medium, a share pasted by hand, a set restored from another
writer — could be handed the attacker's key as the recovered one. A set the
crate's own writer produces never carries such a share; the door is the
reader.

0.8.7 refuses such a set before interpolating (the 0.9 line's next prerelease
carries the same refusal). Where upgrading is not possible, before recovering
split each share on `.` into four fields, base58-decode the x field, and
refuse the set if it decodes to zero (the one-character field `1`, or a value
at or above the field prime) or if two shares carry the same x.

raw.summary: eazip: symlink-target validation checks the wrong argument, allowing extraction path escapes on Windows
raw.details:
When extracting archives, `eazip` validates symlink entries before writing
them. The validation function `validate_symlink()` (`src/utils/mod.rs`) scans
for backslash and NUL bytes, but passes the symlink's *name* where the
symlink's *target* was intended:

```rust
memchr2(b'\\', b'\0', name.as_bytes()) // should be target.as_bytes()
```

As a result, symlink *targets* containing backslash or NUL bytes pass
validation. On Windows, backslash is a path separator, so targets such as
`..\..\..\Windows\system32\evil.exe` also defeat the remaining depth check,
which splits on `/` only. A crafted archive can therefore create symlinks
that resolve outside the extraction directory — including UNC targets such as
`\\host\share\...` — redirecting writes to arbitrary filesystem locations
chosen by the attacker.

Applications that extract untrusted archives with `eazip` on Windows targets
are affected; on Unix targets backslash is not a separator, which limits
exposure there.

The vulnerability was introduced in version 0.2.5 and fixed in 0.2.7
([a1phyr/eazip@0e4caa13](https://github.com/a1phyr/eazip/commit/0e4caa13d59f5ba15aaac332f5534260c3b8fc43)),
which rejects backslash and NUL bytes in the symlink target. It was
privately reported to the maintainer on 2026-11-06 and credited in the
0.2.7 release notes.

raw.summary: Inverted NSEC3 comparison in DNSSEC validation (hickory-proto 0.25)
raw.details:
In hickory-proto 0.25.0 through 0.26.0-alpha.1, DNSSEC validation handled the last NSEC3 record of a zone's hash chain with its two comparisons reversed. That record was treated as covering almost every hash it does not cover, so an attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses could replay it, with its RRSIG, to forge proofs that existing names have no records.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in hickory-proto 0.25 (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor 0.25) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

raw.summary: NSEC3 owner names not checked against the zone in DNSSEC validation (hickory-proto)
raw.details:
Up to 0.26.0-alpha.1, hickory-proto's DNSSEC validation matched NSEC3 records to a name only by the hashed first label of the NSEC3 owner name, without checking that the rest of the owner name was the zone in question. A signed NSEC3 record from any zone the attacker controls could therefore be used, by someone who can answer or modify DNS responses, to prove that a name in another zone does not exist.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in older hickory-proto releases (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

raw.summary: Inverted NSEC3 comparison lets one record "prove" that almost any name does not exist
raw.details:
When DNSSEC validation looks for the NSEC3 record that covers a hashed name, the last record in the zone's hash chain needs special handling, because its next hashed owner name sorts before its own hash. For that record the two comparisons were reversed: it was treated as covering every hash below its owner hash or above its next hash, which is mostly the part of the chain it does not cover.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay that one signed NSEC3 record, with its RRSIG, from the target zone and use it in forged negative answers. The validator then accepts proof that names which do exist have no records.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` (resolver, recursor and client) when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`. The same code was in hickory-proto before it moved to hickory-net.

The fix corrects the comparison in `find_covering_record`. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: RRSIG signer name was not checked against the zone of the signed records
raw.details:
DNSSEC validation checked an RRset against the DNSKEYs of whatever zone was named in the RRSIG's Signer's Name field. RFC 4035 section 5.3.1 requires that name to be the zone that contains the RRset, but this was not checked.

Anyone who controls a DNSSEC-signed zone, and can answer or modify DNS responses, can therefore sign records for names in an unrelated zone with their own keys and have the validator accept them as secure.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` (resolver, recursor and client) when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix ignores an RRSIG whose signer name is not the RRset's owner name or one of its ancestors. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: NSEC wraparound detection trusted an unvalidated SOA record
raw.details:
The last NSEC record in a zone points back to the zone apex. To recognise it, DNSSEC validation treated an NSEC record as covering every name after its owner when its next domain name equalled the owner name of an SOA record in the response. That SOA record did not have to pass validation.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay a genuine NSEC record and its RRSIG, add a forged SOA record whose name equals that NSEC record's next domain name, and so make the validator accept that any name sorting after the NSEC owner does not exist.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix recognises a wraparound NSEC record from the chain itself (its next domain name sorts at or before its owner and is the zone of the queried name) and only uses validated SOA records. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: NSEC3 records from another zone were accepted in proofs of nonexistence
raw.details:
When DNSSEC validation used NSEC3 records to prove that a name or record type does not exist, it compared only the hashed first label of each NSEC3 owner name with the hash of the name being checked. The rest of the owner name, which says which zone the record belongs to, was not checked.

Someone who controls any DNSSEC-signed zone can publish a signed NSEC3 record whose first label is the hash of a name in another zone. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can then use it to make the validator accept that the name in the other zone does not exist.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix requires a matching NSEC3 record to belong to a zone that contains the checked name, and ignores NSEC3 records whose owner is not directly below the RRSIG signer name. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Panic when decoding malformed Ed25519 keys from Base64
raw.details:
In version 0.11.1 and earlier of vodozemac, Ed25519PublicKey::from_base64() and
Ed25519SecretKey::from_base64() panic on malformed input instead of returning an
error, if the input decodes to 31 or 33 bytes instead of the expected 32 bytes.
An attacker who can supply a key to an application using vodozemac can crash it.

## Impact

Ed25519 public keys are routinely received from other Matrix users and servers,
so a malicious party can publish a crafted key that crashes clients parsing it.

The impact is limited to denial of service; no key disclosure or signature
forgery is possible.

raw.summary: NXDOMAIN accepted for a proven empty non-terminal (hickory-proto)
raw.details:
Up to 0.26.0-alpha.1, hickory-proto's NSEC validation accepted an NXDOMAIN response as secure even when the covering NSEC record's next domain name was below the queried name, which proves the name exists as an empty non-terminal. Because the response code is not signed, someone who can modify DNS responses could turn a genuine signed NODATA response into an accepted NXDOMAIN.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in older hickory-proto releases (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

raw.summary: DNSSEC validation accepted an unrelated signed RRset as the answer (hickory-proto)
raw.details:
Up to 0.26.0-alpha.1, hickory-proto's DNSSEC validation treated a response with a non-empty answer section as a positive answer if its records validated, without checking that any of them matched the queried name and type. Someone who can answer or modify DNS responses could return a genuine signed RRset for another name or type and have it accepted as a validated answer.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in older hickory-proto releases (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

raw.summary: Recursor followed every glueless name server in a referral, with no per-query budget
raw.details:
When a referral listed name servers outside the delegated zone and gave no glue addresses, the recursor looked up A and AAAA records for every listed name server, recursing into each one. Only the chain-depth limits applied. There was no cap on how many name servers it chased per referral or on the total upstream work per client query.

Someone who controls a zone can return referrals that list many glueless name servers in a victim's domain, and nest them, so that each client query makes the recursor send a large number of queries to the victim's servers (the NXNSAttack pattern). The same can exhaust the recursor's own resources.

This affects the recursive resolver, which is in hickory-resolver behind the opt-in `recursor` feature from 0.26.0-beta.1. Earlier releases shipped it as the separate hickory-recursor crate.

From 0.26.2 the recursor follows at most 5 glueless name servers per delegation and sends at most 200 upstream queries per client request.

raw.summary: Recursor kept querying cyclic glueless sibling delegations
raw.details:
Two zones can each delegate to name servers named only inside the other zone, with no glue records (the cyclic sibling case in RFC 9471 section 2.3). Such delegations can never be resolved, but the recursor did not stop when it came back to a zone it was already resolving. It kept sending queries until the per-request limits ran out, and zero TTLs on the referral NS records made this worse.

Someone who controls two such zones can make a recursor send many upstream queries for each client query.

This affects the recursive resolver, which is in hickory-resolver behind the opt-in `recursor` feature from 0.26.0-beta.1. Earlier releases shipped it as the separate hickory-recursor crate.

From 0.26.2 each client request tracks the zones on its resolution stack and refuses to enter a zone that is already on it.

raw.summary: Spoofed malformed UDP datagrams abort DNS lookups
raw.details:
While waiting for a reply on a UDP connection, the client parsed every datagram that arrived from the name server's address and port before checking its message ID. If parsing failed, the attempt ended with an error instead of dropping the datagram and waiting for the real reply. The receive loop also gave up after three datagrams.

An off-path attacker who can guess the client's source port, but not the transaction ID, can send one malformed datagram with a spoofed source address and make the pending lookup fail.

The fix reads the message ID from the first two bytes before parsing, ignores short datagrams and datagrams with the wrong ID, keeps listening until the outer timeout, and only then parses the response. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: DNSSEC validation cache could reuse an Insecure result for a different name
raw.details:
The DNSSEC validation cache used a 64-bit hash of the query as its key, and two keys with the same hash counted as equal. The `Hash` implementation of `Name` hashed the bytes of the labels but not where one label ends and the next begins, so names that differ only in the placement of dots (such as `ab.c.` and `a.bc.`) hashed to the same value.

An attacker who controls an unsigned delegation whose name collides in this way with a name in a signed zone can first get an Insecure result cached for their own name. A forged response for the signed name is then served from that cache entry without signature checks and returned with the AD bit clear, where validation should have failed.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix stores the query in the cache key and compares it on lookup. The `Hash` implementations of `Label`, `Name` and `LowerName` in hickory-proto were also changed to include label boundaries. Both are in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: NXDOMAIN accepted for an empty non-terminal that the NSEC record proves exists
raw.details:
When an NSEC record's next domain name is below the queried name, the queried name exists as an empty non-terminal (RFC 8020 section 3.1). The NSEC validator did not check for this case and accepted an NXDOMAIN response backed by such a record as secure.

The response code is not covered by any signature. An attacker who can modify DNS responses can take a genuine signed NODATA response for an empty non-terminal, change its response code to NXDOMAIN, and have the validator accept that an existing name does not exist.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix rejects NXDOMAIN as bogus, and validates NODATA as secure, when the covering NSEC record's next domain name is below the queried name and is not the zone apex. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: DNSSEC validation accepted a validly signed but unrelated RRset as the answer
raw.details:
When a response had a non-empty answer section, DNSSEC validation treated it as a positive answer as long as the records in it validated. It did not check that any of those records had the queried name and either the queried type or type CNAME.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can therefore return a genuine, signed RRset for some other name or type, and have it accepted as a validated answer to the query instead of being handled as a response with no matching data.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix requires at least one answer record that matches the query name and is either of the queried type or a CNAME, both for positive responses and when NSEC records are checked. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Recursor followed every glueless name server in a referral (no fixed hickory-recursor release)
raw.details:
For referrals whose name servers are outside the delegated zone and come without glue, the recursor resolved every listed name server, with no cap on referral width and no per-query work budget. Someone who controls a zone can use this to make each client query send a large number of queries to a victim's servers (the NXNSAttack pattern), or to exhaust the recursor.

The recursor code moved into hickory-resolver (opt-in `recursor` feature) in 0.26.0-beta.1, and the fix is in hickory-resolver 0.26.2. No hickory-recursor release contains a fix, so users should move to hickory-resolver 0.26.2 or later with the `recursor` feature.

raw.summary: Recursor kept querying cyclic glueless sibling delegations (no fixed hickory-recursor release)
raw.details:
Two zones can each delegate to name servers named only inside the other zone, with no glue records (RFC 9471 section 2.3). The recursor did not stop when it came back to a zone it was already resolving, so someone who controls two such zones can make it send many upstream queries for each client query.

The recursor code moved into hickory-resolver (opt-in `recursor` feature) in 0.26.0-beta.1, and the fix is in hickory-resolver 0.26.2. No hickory-recursor release contains a fix, so users should move to hickory-resolver 0.26.2 or later with the `recursor` feature.

raw.summary: MAX_STREAM_DATA frame can open streams beyond the stream limit
raw.details:
When a MAX_STREAM_DATA frame named a peer-initiated bidirectional stream that was not open yet, `received_max_stream_data` treated the stream, and every lower-numbered stream, as opened without checking the stream ID against the limit advertised to the peer. RFC 9000 section 4.6 requires closing the connection with `STREAM_LIMIT_ERROR` in this case, and the STREAM and RESET_STREAM handlers already did so.

After the handshake, a peer can send one small MAX_STREAM_DATA frame naming a very large stream index, and `accept` then yields every stream up to that index. In `quinn`, a loop that keeps calling `accept_bi` can be handed more than 2^40 streams. Depending on the runtime, the endpoint runs out of memory, stops accepting new connections, or keeps busy indefinitely, even after the peer has gone away. Clients and servers that accept peer-initiated bidirectional streams are affected. Unidirectional streams are not.

The fix validates the stream ID in `received_max_stream_data` and adds a defensive check where streams are opened implicitly. It is in 0.11.19.

raw.summary: Long Retry token can panic or exhaust memory in a QUIC client
raw.details:
A client kept the token from a Retry packet without any length limit and put it into the header of every Initial packet it sent afterwards. Initial datagrams are 1200 bytes. When the token and connection IDs left no room for the minimum payload, `PacketBuilder::new` computed a minimum packet size larger than the maximum, which only a debug assertion checked. On the next `poll_transmit`, debug builds panic, and release builds try to allocate more than 10 GiB in one call. With longer tokens the allocation fails and the process aborts.

A matching Retry packet can be built from the client's first Initial alone. The attacker can therefore be the server being contacted, or anyone who sees that Initial and can answer before the server does. Every application that makes outgoing connections with `quinn-proto` is affected, including all `quinn` clients. Servers do not process Retry packets.

The fix closes the connection with `PROTOCOL_VIOLATION` when an Initial token leaves too little room for frames. That covers Retry tokens and cached address-validation tokens, since both come from the peer. It also reserves room for CONNECTION_CLOSE after large Initial headers. Both changes are in 0.11.19.

raw.summary: UB can be reached from safe code
raw.details:
The variance of `RefSwap` and `OptionRefSwap` were incorrect, possibly allowing use-after-free.

`OptionRefSwap::into_inner` did not check for null.

The fix is to make `RefSwap` and `OptionRefSwap` invariant, and to change `OptionRefSwap::into_inner` to return an option.
It is available in version 0.1.3.
If your project still compiles with 0.1.3 then it is not affected by the unsoundness on version 0.1.2

raw.summary: KVStoreInterpreter::verify_signature_legacy answers true for every token and every key
raw.details:
`KVStoreInterpreter::verify_signature_legacy(&PushDrop, &PublicKey)`, public
and deprecated since 0.2.0 (the crate's first release), read neither argument
and answered `true`. A KVStore token signed by nobody, a signed token checked
against a key other than its controller's, and a PushDrop with no fields each
passed. Its documentation said it delegated to the `KVStoreFields`-based
verifier; it did not.

An application that checks, with this function, a KVStore token it did not
write (an overlay lookup's answer, or a transaction output a peer hands it) and
acts on `true` accepts a value no controller signed, attributed to whatever
controller the token names. No caller in the crate itself uses the function.
This was run on 0.2.0, 0.5.0, 0.8.0, 0.8.7, 0.8.8, 0.9.0-beta.1 and
0.9.0-beta.7 as crates.io serves them, and the source of all 63 published
versions carries the same constant body (the yanked 0.3.21 included).

0.8.9 answers `true` only for a token whose controller field is the
given key and whose last field is that key's signature over the others (the
0.9 line's next prerelease carries the same fix). There is no workaround:
upgrade to 0.8.9, or, on the 0.9 line, to its next prerelease.

raw.summary: Parent-side NSEC at a zone cut accepted as proof of nonexistence (hickory-proto)
raw.details:
Up to 0.26.0-alpha.1, hickory-proto's DNSSEC validation accepted the NSEC record that a parent zone signs at a delegation as proof that names below the zone cut, or other types at the cut, do not exist. Such a record only proves that no DS record exists there (RFC 6840 section 4.1). Someone who can answer or modify DNS responses could replay the parent's genuine signed records to get a denial for an existing name in the child zone accepted as secure.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in older hickory-proto releases (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

raw.summary: Child-side NSEC or NSEC3 record accepted as proof that a delegation has no DS record (hickory-proto)
raw.details:
Up to 0.26.0-alpha.1, hickory-proto's DNSSEC validation accepted an NSEC or NSEC3 record from the child side of a zone cut, which has the SOA bit set, as proof that the parent has no DS record for the delegation (RFC 4035 section 5.2, RFC 6840 section 4.4). Someone who can answer or modify DNS responses could make a secure delegation look insecure and then forge records in the child zone.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in older hickory-proto releases (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

raw.summary: Parent-side NSEC3 at a zone cut accepted as proof of nonexistence (hickory-proto 0.25)
raw.details:
In hickory-proto 0.25.0 through 0.26.0-alpha.1, NSEC3 validation picked the closest encloser by hashed owner name alone and accepted the NSEC3 record that a parent zone signs at a delegation as proof that names at or below the zone cut do not exist. Such a record only proves that no DS record exists there (RFC 6840 section 4.1, RFC 5155 section 8.3). Someone who can answer or modify DNS responses could replay the parent's genuine signed records to get a denial for an existing name in the child zone accepted as secure.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in hickory-proto 0.25 (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor 0.25) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

raw.summary: Incorrect handling of embedded SVG and MathML leads to mutation XSS
raw.details:
The MathML text integration points (`mi`, `mo`, `mn`, `ms`, `mtext`) and SVG `foreignObject` can be made to contain a tag in the other one's namespace (a MathML integration point with a child in the SVG namespace, or vice versa) without the root tag that switches out of the HTML namespace. If the attacker can construct input that parses differently in as HTML than as foreign XML, they can inject arbitrary JavaScript code into the user's browser.

For example:

- The user writes `<math><mi><svg><gadget></svg></mi></math>`.
- The application enables `math`, `mi`, and the gadget, but not `svg`.
- Ammonia filters the input to `<math><mi><gadget></mi></math>`.
- Because svg is now gone, the gadget switches from being parsed as SVG to being parsed as HTML.
- The gadget is written in such a way that it exploits the parsing differences between HTML and MathML.

As far as we know, the gadget can only be written using a tag that is parsed as raw text in HTML. These [elements] are:

- title
- textarea
- xmp
- iframe
- noembed
- noframes
- plaintext
- noscript
- style
- script

Applications that do not explicitly allow any of these tags should not be affected, since none are allowed by default.

[elements]: https://github.com/servo/html5ever/blob/a027c2835472d518893c906dc29c42200af3c960/html5ever/src/tree_builder/rules.rs

---

This vulnerability was reported by Roger Meyer.

raw.summary: Unbounded backoff state from PRUNE messages for unknown topics
raw.details:
A PRUNE control message names topics and asks for a backoff on each. The handler recorded a backoff for every named topic, including topics the local node had never joined. A peer can send PRUNEs naming many new short topic IDs with a long backoff. Each pair is kept until the backoff expires, up to an hour, even after the peer disconnects, so a stream of PRUNEs, possibly from many peer IDs, can use up the node's memory. Peer scoring does not penalise these messages.

The fix ignores PRUNE entries for topics that are not in the node's mesh. It is in 0.50.1, and was backported to the main branch in libp2p/rust-libp2p#6707.

raw.summary: Unbounded memory growth from GRAFT messages for unsubscribed topics
raw.details:
When a GRAFT control message arrived, every topic it named was added to that peer's set of topics, on the assumption that a peer grafting us must be subscribed. Nothing checked that the peer had subscribed, and subscription filters only apply to SUBSCRIBE messages. A peer can keep sending GRAFTs with new short topic IDs over one connection, and the set grows until the peer unsubscribes or disconnects. Memory grows without bound and the node can be killed for running out of memory.

The fix no longer records topics from GRAFT messages and drops a GRAFT for a topic the peer has not subscribed to. It also makes `MaxCountSubscriptionFilter` the default subscription filter. It is in 0.49.5, and was backported to the 0.50 line before 0.50.0.

raw.summary: Receive loop can spin after a truncated datagram
raw.details:
Some targets read one datagram per `recvmsg` call instead of using `recvmmsg`: Apple platforms without the `fast-apple-datapath` feature, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Solaris and illumos, and from 0.6 also DragonFly BSD, Redox and GNU/Hurd. On these targets the receive loop set up its `msghdr` only once and looked at the `MSG_TRUNC` flag before checking whether `recvmsg` had failed. After a datagram larger than the receive buffer was dropped, a following `EAGAIN` still saw the old truncation flag. The loop then kept issuing non-blocking receives instead of returning `WouldBlock`.

When the receive buffer is smaller than a datagram that arrives, a remote sender can keep the task that drives the socket busy, before any QUIC packet authentication. The loop ends only when a later datagram fits in the buffer. Whether an application is exposed therefore depends on the receive buffer size it uses. Linux, Android, FreeBSD and Windows use other receive paths and are not affected.

The fix rebuilds the header before every `recvmsg` call and returns receive errors before checking the truncation flag. It is in 0.5.16 and 0.6.3.

raw.summary: Parent-side NSEC at a zone cut accepted as proof of nonexistence below the cut
raw.details:
At a delegation, the parent zone signs an NSEC record for the child's name whose type bitmap has NS but not SOA (or has DNAME). RFC 6840 section 4.1 says such a record only proves that no DS record exists at that name. It says nothing about names below the cut or about other types at the cut, because those belong to the child zone.

DNSSEC validation did not make this distinction. It used such a record as a covering NSEC for names below the cut, and as a direct match proving that other types did not exist at the cut. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay the parent's genuine signed records to get an NXDOMAIN or NODATA response for an existing name in the child zone accepted as secure. A recursor caches that denial for the negative TTL.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix adds `NSEC::is_ancestor_delegation()` in hickory-proto. Validation no longer uses such a record to cover a name below its owner, and treats a direct match on it as bogus unless the query is for DS. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Child-side NSEC or NSEC3 record accepted as proof that a delegation has no DS record
raw.details:
To show that a delegation is insecure, a validator needs proof that the parent zone has no DS record for it. That proof must come from the parent side of the zone cut: RFC 4035 section 5.2, RFC 5155 section 8.9 and RFC 6840 section 4.4 require the matching NSEC or NSEC3 record not to have the SOA bit set, since a record with SOA comes from the child zone's apex.

DNSSEC validation did not check this. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can answer a DS query with the child zone's own signed NSEC or NSEC3 record for its apex, which does not list DS, and have the validator accept that the delegation is insecure. Records in the child zone can then be forged without any signature.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix treats a NODATA proof for a DS query as bogus when the directly matching NSEC or NSEC3 record has SOA in its type bitmap. It is in 0.26.2.

raw.summary: Parent-side NSEC3 at a zone cut accepted as proof of nonexistence at and below the cut
raw.details:
At a delegation, the parent zone signs an NSEC3 record for the child's name whose type bitmap has NS but not SOA (or has DNAME). RFC 6840 section 4.1 and RFC 5155 section 8.3 say such a record only proves that no DS record exists at that name.

NSEC3 validation picked the closest encloser by matching the hashed owner name alone, without looking at the type bitmap, so it accepted such a record as the closest encloser for names below the cut. For NODATA responses, it accepted a direct match on such a record as proof that any type other than the queried one and CNAME was absent, not only DS. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay the parent's genuine signed records to get an NXDOMAIN for a name below the cut, or a NODATA for a non-DS type at the cut, accepted as secure. A recursor caches that denial for the negative TTL.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix adds `NSEC3::is_ancestor_delegation()` in hickory-proto. Validation no longer accepts such a record as a closest encloser, and treats a direct match on it as bogus unless the query is for DS. It is in 0.26.2.
